newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile miners may strike to protest privatizations.
newsitem.headline: Chile miners may strike to protest privatizations.

text.p: Chilean state copper workers will consider calling strike action to protest the government's reported plans to privatize parts of state oil company Enap and state metals smelting firm Enami, union leaders said.

The Confederation of Copper Workers, which claims 17,000 members, agreed with union leaders from Enap (Empresa Nacional del Petoleo) and Enami (Empresa Nacional de Mineria) to coordinate protest actions in case the government announces any privatizations, they said.

"We have signed an agreement with the unions of Enap and Enami. What happens now all depends on what the government announces, and we will decide what actions to take," confederation president Raimundo Espinosa said. Asked if that could include strikes, he said yes.

President Eduardo Frei will announce plans to sell a controlling stake in two oil refineries, in Concon and Concepcion, both owned by Enap, possibly as early as his annual speech to Congress on May 21, government sources have said.

News reports have also said Enami may also sell stakes in its smelter at Paipote and a smelter and refinery complex in Ventanas, though not necessarily majority stakes nor at the same time as the Enap sales.
Any privatization at Enami in particular would spark labor unrest that would dwarf that which followed the closure of state-owned Lota coal mine last month, said Espinosa.

"If they try to privatize Enami, they're going to get into a conflict three times greater than Lota," he told a news conference. "To privatize Enami would be to eliminate all support for small and medium- sized mines."

Enami buys concentrates from small private mines at prices that allow them to operate economically, leading critics to call it essentially a state subsidy for small copper pits that would otherwise go under.
The privatizations, if they happen, would be the most important rollback of the Chilean state's role in the economy since the country ended 17 years of military rule in 1990.

The confederation, representing workers only in Codelco and Enami, sees the selloffs as the first step toward privatizing Codelco although Frei's government has insisted it plans no sale of Codelco's mines.
"The private mining companies want to sink their teeth into Codelco and we the workers are not going to allow it," said confederation national secretary Manuel Rodriguez.

Frei is constitutionally barred from privatizing Codelco's wholly- owned mines, even if he wanted to. But the government sold Codelco's power plant in Tocopilla and there have been reports it may sell part of its 49 percent stake in the El Abra copper project or other smaller assets to raise money.
